---
title: "Data Splitting and Feature Engineering"
---

This lecture bridges statistical modeling and practical machine
learning workflows: split data correctly, prepare features reproducibly,
and avoid leakage.

## Learning Objectives

- Create training, validation, and test partitions.
- Identify leakage in preprocessing and feature construction.
- Encode categorical variables and transform skewed predictors.
- Build preprocessing steps that can be applied to future data.

## Core Ideas

Feature engineering is part of the model. Any operation that learns from
the data must be estimated on the training set and applied unchanged to
validation or test data.

## Worked Example

Use the Ames housing data to demonstrate:

- partitioning,
- missingness checks,
- transformations,
- dummy variables,
- model-ready data objects.

## Partitioning Patterns

Data can be split with base R, `caret`, `rsample`, H2O, and other
modeling frameworks. Teach the principle first, then show one modern
implementation in detail.

```r
library(rsample)

set.seed(571)
ames_split <- initial_split(ames, prop = 0.8, strata = SalePrice)
ames_train <- training(ames_split)
ames_test <- testing(ames_split)
```

The point of stratification is to keep the response distribution roughly
comparable across training and testing data. This is especially useful
when the outcome is imbalanced or heavily skewed.

## Feature Engineering Checklist

A practical feature engineering checklist includes:

| Step | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Transform skewed variables | Make relationships easier for simple models to capture. |
| Scale numeric features | Put predictors on comparable scales for distance- or penalty-based methods. |
| Bin carefully | Convert continuous variation into interpretable groups only when it helps. |
| Lump rare levels | Reduce instability from sparse categorical levels. |
| Encode categorical variables | Create model-ready features without inventing ordinal meaning. |
| Handle missing values | Make missingness explicit and reproducible. |

All of these steps must be learned from the training data and then
applied to future data. That is the anti-leakage rule.

```r
library(recipes)

ames_recipe <-
  recipe(SalePrice ~ ., data = ames_train) |>
  step_log(SalePrice, base = 10, skip = TRUE) |>
  step_other(all_nominal_predictors(), threshold = 0.01) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())
```

## Interactions as Feature Construction

An interaction lets the effect of one predictor depend on the value of
another:

$$
\operatorname{E}(Y \mid X, Z) =
\beta_0 + \beta_1X + \beta_2Z + \beta_3XZ.
$$

The marginal effect of $X$ is then

$$
\frac{\partial \operatorname{E}(Y \mid X, Z)}{\partial X}
= \beta_1 + \beta_3Z.
$$

Once an interaction enters the model, the main effect of $X$ is
conditional on the value of $Z$.
